incremental_to: Sharpe 0.95 against 1.53 (Qwen-1.5-1.8B-Chat) and 1.76 (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct); authors read this as at least 54% to 62% of predictability surviving without leakage

citation: Yan, Tang, Gao, Jiang and Lu (2026), DatedGPT: Preventing Lookahead Bias in Large Language Models with Time-Aware Pretraining, arXiv 2603.11838 v2
text_source: Over 61,000 firm-day news headlines

citation: Aavang, Tjalk-Bøggild, Iolov, Rizzi, Zhang & Bjerva (2026), ACL 2026 Industry Track, pp. 1434-1460

citation: Ju, Huang, Lin, Lin & Wang (2023), ACL 2023 Long Papers, pp. 14307-14321

informs_decision: Method comparison: same development set and same number of development evaluations; fine-tuning factor on the same base model

citation: Staab, Vero, Balunović and Vechev (2024), Beyond Memorization: Violating Privacy via Inference with Large Language Models, ICLR 2024 (spotlight), arXiv 2310.07298 v2 (HTML read)

citation: Staab, Vero, Balunović and Vechev (2025), Language Models are Advanced Anonymizers, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2402.13846 v2 (v1 titled Large Language Models are Advanced Anonymizers; HTML read)

citation: Yang, Zhu and Gurevych (2025), Robust Utility-Preserving Text Anonymization Based on Large Language Models, ACL 2025, arXiv 2407.11770 v2 (HTML read)

citation: Krčo, Yao, Meeus and de Montjoye (2026), RAT-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Text Anonymization, arXiv 2602.12806 v1 (HTML read, first 100,000 characters)
text_source: Synthetic GPT-4.1 transcripts and chats (100 English, 50 Spanish, 50 Chinese) embedding census-sampled indirect identifiers and one direct identifier

citation: Zhou, Mireshghallah and Li (2025), Operationalizing Data Minimization for Privacy-Preserving LLM Prompting, arXiv 2510.03662 v1 (HTML read, first 100,000 characters; ICLR 2026 poster page not opened)
text_source: ShareGPT (176), WildChat (139), MedQA (108), CaseHOLD (110) prompts; nine target LLMs
feature: Minimal disclosure: per sensitive span, retain, abstract or redact, subject to task utility
method: Priority-queue tree search from the most protective profile, relaxing one span at a time until utility passes (correct in 5 of 5 runs, or GPT-4o judge); attacker recovery audit; models also asked to predict the minimum

pit_handling: Not addressed; for multiple-choice tasks the oracle uses the correct answer
informs_decision: Q1/Q2: template design as a minimisation search; stronger models need less (gpt-5 85.7% redacted v qwen2.5-0.5b 19.3%); redaction protects better than abstraction (recovery 2.7-7.7% v 5.6-14.9%); models overshare when asked what they need; oracle must use non-memorised labels

citation: Wu, Wu and Zou (2024), ClashEval: Quantifying the Tug-of-War between an LLM's Internal Prior and External Evidence, arXiv 2404.10198 v2 and v3 (HTML read); a search result lists it in the NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks proceedings (not opened)
text_source: 1,294 questions in six domains with correct and perturbed reference documents (numeric answers times 0.1 to 10; dates shifted; names altered)
feature: Whether the answer follows the document or the model's prior

outcome: Accuracy, context bias, prior bias, context preference rate
pit_handling: Measures the mechanism (parametric knowledge against in-context text), not dated leakage
informs_decision: Q2: with a correct document a strong model rarely keeps a wrong prior (Claude Opus prior bias 0.021), so quote-checked numbers are the safe part; with an altered document Opus resists it most (context bias 0.157), so never give an informed extractor noised numbers; confident priors win where the document is silent

citation: de Montjoye, Hidalgo, Verleysen and Blondel (2013), Unique in the Crowd: The Privacy Bounds of Human Mobility, Scientific Reports 3, 1376 (PMC copy read)
text_source: Mobile-phone traces of about 1.5 million users, 15 months, about 6,500 antennas

outcome: Share of users uniquely identified
informs_decision: Q4: coarsening has weak returns (halving resolution cuts identification by 9.3% with four points, 6.2% with ten; 'even coarse datasets provide little anonymity'); remove fields rather than round them

citation: Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019), Estimating the success of re-identifications in incomplete datasets using generative models, Nature Communications 10, 3069 (PMC copy read)
text_source: Census and survey corpora including US (Massachusetts) data, sampled 0.1% to 100%
feature: Per-record probability of population uniqueness and of a correct match
method: Latent Gaussian copula fitted to a sample; closed forms xi = 1 - p(x)^(n-1) and kappa = (1/(n p(x)))(1 - (1 - p(x))^n)
outcome: MAE and AUC of estimated uniqueness; share unique given k attributes
informs_decision: Q4: a code-only risk per brief with the S&P 500 as the population; 15 attributes make 99.98% of Massachusetts residents unique; sampling gives no protection; used by RAT-Bench

citation: Qian, Wang, Peng and twelve others including Lopez-Lira and Tang (2026), LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting (FinDendro), arXiv 2611.06808 v1 (HTML read)

citation: Lopez-Lira, Tang and Zhu (2025), The Memorization Problem: Can We Trust LLMs' Economic Forecasts?, arXiv 2504.14765 v2; sections 5.6, 5.7 and appendix A.7 re-read for this stream (the existing note lopez-lira-2025-memorization-problem.md does not cover section 5.7)

text_source: Compustat annual and quarterly data for 149 US retailers 1994-2004; store counts from 10-Ks; consumer sentiment; I/B/E/S sales forecasts
feature: Inventory per store and gross margin, modelled jointly with sales per store
method: Three simultaneous equations with curve shifters; reduced-form forecasts; fit 1994-2003, test 2004
outcome: Sales revenue per store
incremental_to: ARIMA(1,1,1) MAPE 8.62% and augmented time series 6.41% vs model 5.82%; analysts on 42 firms 6.36% vs 2.45% (working paper)
pit_handling: Not discussed; working-paper ex-post forecasts use the target year's exogenous variables and store count, and analysts' forecasts are 13 months old (our reading)
informs_decision: Q(a): inventory relative to sales and gross margin bear on retailer revenue; the accuracy edge is not point in time, so treat it as optimistic; retailers only, annual

citation: Toynbee (2017), Implications of Disclosing Order Backlog, PhD dissertation, University of Washington; deposited version read
text_source: 10-K order backlog (Regulation S-K Item 1); Compustat and CRSP; 15 manufacturing industries 1996-2014
feature: Percentage change in backlog intensity (backlog over sales); inventory over sales
method: Pooled OLS with firm and year clustering; Vuong tests; ERC, investment and persistence tests with propensity matching
outcome: Next-year sales growth; next-year earnings; RNOA persistence
incremental_to: Inventory growth only (no control for current or past sales growth): backlog R2 9.9% vs inventory 2.3%, both 10.5%
informs_decision: Q(a): the clearest backlog-to-revenue number (R2 about 10%, manufacturers, annual); stronger for make-to-order; backlog is much broader than deferred revenue; incremental value over past growth untested

citation: Dechow, Richardson and Sloan (2008), The Persistence and Pricing of the Cash Component of Earnings, Journal of Accounting Research; working paper of December 2004 read
text_source: Compustat 1950-2003, 254,596 firm-years; 150,837 with CRSP returns
feature: Accruals vs cash flows; cash split into change in cash, debt and equity distributions
method: Annual cross-sectional persistence regressions (Fama-MacBeth); Mishkin tests
outcome: Next-year income over assets
incremental_to: Income alone 0.657; accruals 0.606 vs free cash flow 0.681; adjusted R2 0.424 to 0.464
informs_decision: Q(b) EPS label only: the accrual effect is real but small on annual ROA; equity distributions explain the cash premium; earnings persistence has fallen over time

citation: Curtis, Lundholm and McVay (2014), Forecasting Sales: A Model and Some Evidence from the Retail Industry, Contemporary Accounting Research 31(2) 581-608; abstract read
text_source: Retail firms' public disclosures (store counts, comparable-store growth)
feature: Sales growth split into growth in sales-generating units (new stores) and growth in the sales rate of existing units (comparable stores); new stores may earn more or less
method: Structural sales model on a few years of firm data
outcome: Sales
incremental_to: Analyst revenue forecasts: out-of-sample nearly as accurate; combined with analysts significantly more accurate than analysts alone
informs_decision: Q(a): units times rate (and by analogy volume vs price, organic vs acquired) is the best-supported revenue decomposition; in-sample errors under 2% of sales

citation: Bernard and Noel (1991), Do Inventory Disclosures Predict Sales and Earnings?, Journal of Accounting, Auditing and Finance 6(2); abstract read
text_source: Inventory disclosures by component (raw materials, work in process, finished goods)
feature: Unexpected inventory changes after controlling for current sales
method: Time-series prediction beyond current and past sales and earnings
outcome: Future sales and earnings
incremental_to: Current and past values of sales and earnings
informs_decision: Q(a)/(b): manufacturers' raw materials and WIP lead sales positively (earnings neutral); finished goods do not lead sales and lead earnings negatively; retailers' inventory leads earnings negatively and sales only briefly

citation: Abarbanell and Bushee (1998), Abnormal Returns to a Fundamental Analysis Strategy, The Accounting Review; abstract read
text_source: Annual financial statements
feature: Signals: changes in inventories, receivables, gross margin, selling expenses, capex, effective tax rate, inventory method, audit qualification, labour productivity
method: Portfolio formation on combined signals
outcome: 12-month size-adjusted returns; earnings news
pit_handling: Holdout period after the signals were published still earns returns
informs_decision: Q(b): the standard signal list; returns of 13.2% concentrate around later earnings announcements and vanish after one year, so the signals bear on next-year earnings, not long-run growth

citation: Rajgopal, Shevlin and Venkatachalam (2003), Does the Stock Market Fully Appreciate the Implications of Leading Indicators for Future Earnings? Evidence from Order Backlog, Review of Accounting Studies 8(4); abstract read
text_source: Order backlog disclosures
feature: Order backlog
method: Prediction and pricing (Mishkin-type) tests; hedge portfolio
outcome: Future earnings; returns
informs_decision: Q(a)/(b): backlog predicts future earnings; the market overweights it (a search summary said 'underweights'; the abstract says overweights); mispricing is not due to analysts

citation: Banker, Barber, Hollie and Park (2019), Contingent Information Content of Order Backlog and the Direction of Sales Change, conference paper, ScholarSpace (University of Hawaii); abstract read
text_source: Order backlog relative to average assets
feature: Backlog level, interacted with the direction of the current sales change
method: Regressions of future sales direction, earnings and returns
outcome: Probability of a future sales decrease; earnings; price
informs_decision: Q(a): the more backlog, the less likely next-period sales fall; above the median backlog a current sales decrease is no longer bad news (direction of sales, close to S2's label)

citation: Kesavan and Mani (2013), The Relationship Between Abnormal Inventory Growth and Future Earnings for U.S. Public Retailers, Manufacturing and Service Operations Management 15(1) 6-23; abstract read
text_source: Retailer financial statements
feature: Abnormal inventory growth against operations benchmarks
method: Regressions; analyst bias tests; portfolios
outcome: One-year-ahead EPS; analyst errors; returns
incremental_to: Analyst EPS forecasts (systematically biased with respect to abnormal inventory growth)
informs_decision: Q(b): inverted-U between abnormal inventory growth and next-year EPS: both too little and too much inventory hurt; EPS label only

citation: Prakash and Sinha (2013), Deferred Revenues and the Matching of Revenues and Expenses, Contemporary Accounting Research (online 2012); abstract read
text_source: Deferred revenue liability (nearly 40% of industrial firms 2002-2009, averaging at least 10% of sales)
feature: Change in revenue deferrals
method: Predictability, analyst-error and pricing tests
outcome: Future earnings; analyst sales and margin forecast errors
incremental_to: Analyst sales and margin forecasts (err in the direction of the deferral change)
informs_decision: Q(a)/(b): rising deferrals depress current sales and margins and inflate future ones; analysts underestimate future earnings when deferrals rise; a revenue and margin lead

citation: Zhong, Wang and Ning (2016), Implications of Deferred Revenue Changes for Future Financial Performance and Market Underreaction, Quarterly Journal of Finance and Accounting 54(3-4) 65-100; abstract read (CWU repository page)
text_source: Current deferred revenues
feature: Change in current deferred revenue
method: Regressions of future performance; valuation and return tests
outcome: Sales growth, gross margin, profit margin, ROA
informs_decision: Q(a): deferred revenue changes lead sales growth and margins over two years; investors underreact

citation: Doyle, Lundholm and Soliman (2003), The Predictive Value of Expenses Excluded from Pro Forma Earnings, Review of Accounting Studies 8(2); abstract read
text_source: Pro forma (street) earnings vs GAAP
feature: Expenses excluded from pro forma earnings
method: Prediction and trading tests
outcome: Future cash flows; returns
informs_decision: Q(b) EPS label: 'one-off' exclusions are not unimportant: higher exclusions predict lower future cash flows and the market misses it

citation: Burgstahler, Jiambalvo and Shevlin (2002), Do Stock Prices Fully Reflect the Implications of Special Items for Future Earnings?, Journal of Accounting Research; abstract read
text_source: Quarterly earnings
feature: Special items component of quarterly earnings
method: Two-equation (prediction and pricing) tests; abnormal returns
outcome: Future quarterly earnings; returns
informs_decision: Q(b) EPS label: special items are largely but not wholly transitory, and prices do not fully reflect it; a strategy on their sign earns small 3-day returns four quarters later

citation: Dechow and Ge (2006), The Persistence of Earnings and Cash Flows and the Role of Special Items: Implications for the Accrual Anomaly, Review of Accounting Studies 11(2); abstract read
text_source: Annual financial statements
feature: Accrual sign and size; special items
method: Persistence regressions by accrual group; returns
outcome: Future earnings; returns
incremental_to: Cash flows; analyst coverage and institutional holdings (returns)
informs_decision: Q(b) EPS label: accruals raise persistence in high-accrual firms and lower it in low-accrual firms, where special items drive the low persistence

citation: Banker and Chen (2006), Predicting Earnings Using a Model Based on Cost Variability and Cost Stickiness, The Accounting Review 81(2) 285ff; abstract read
text_source: Compustat income statements
feature: Cost variability with sales and cost stickiness on sales declines
method: Earnings forecast model benchmarked against two line-item models
outcome: One-year-ahead ROE
incremental_to: Operating/non-operating and cash/accrual line-item models (beaten); analysts' consensus (not beaten)
informs_decision: Q(b) EPS label: when sales fall, costs fall less; useful for margin and EPS given a revenue view, not for revenue itself

citation: Fairfield and Yohn (2001), Using Asset Turnover and Profit Margin to Forecast Changes in Profitability, Review of Accounting Studies; abstract read
text_source: Annual financial statements
feature: Level and change of asset turnover and profit margin
method: Forecast regressions
outcome: Change in ROA
informs_decision: Q(b): splitting the ROA level adds nothing; the change in asset turnover does help forecast next-year ROA change (EPS-side only)

citation: Fairfield, Ramnath and Yohn (2009), Do Industry-Level Analyses Improve Forecasts of Financial Performance?, Journal of Accounting Research; abstract read
text_source: Annual financial statements
feature: Industry-specific vs economy-wide mean reversion
method: Out-of-sample forecast comparison
outcome: Firm growth and profitability
informs_decision: Q(a): industry-specific models forecast firm growth better (not profitability); supports a sector-relative growth feature in code

citation: Chan, Karceski and Lakonishok (2003), The Level and Persistence of Growth Rates, Journal of Finance 58(2) 643-684; abstract read
text_source: Compustat and I/B/E/S
feature: Past long-term growth; I/B/E/S long-term growth forecasts; valuation ratios
method: Persistence and predictability tests
outcome: Long-term growth in earnings and other operating measures
informs_decision: Q(a) what is not predictive: no persistence in long-term earnings growth beyond chance; I/B/E/S growth forecasts optimistic and add little; valuation ratios weak

citation: Foster (1977), Quarterly Accounting Data: Time-Series Properties and Predictive-Ability Results, The Accounting Review; abstract read
text_source: Quarterly earnings, sales and expenses of 69 firms, 1946-1974
feature: Box-Jenkins models with adjacent-quarter and seasonal components
method: One-step-ahead forecasts
outcome: Next-quarter sales, expenses, earnings
informs_decision: Q(a) baseline: quarterly sales have an adjacent-quarter and a seasonal component modelled at firm level; the comparison-base rule is this structure, the baseline any signal must beat

citation: Thomas and Zhang (2002), Inventory Changes and Future Returns, Review of Accounting Studies; abstract read
text_source: Annual financial statements
feature: Inventory changes within accruals
method: Decomposition of the accrual anomaly; extreme decile regularities
outcome: Future returns; profitability reversals
informs_decision: Q(b): the accrual-return relation is mainly inventory changes; the authors speculate demand shifts and impending profitability reversals, possibly masked by earnings management

citation: Ertimur, Livnat and Martikainen (2003), Differential Market Reactions to Revenue and Expense Surprises, Review of Accounting Studies; abstract read
text_source: Preliminary earnings announcements
feature: Revenue surprise vs expense surprise
method: Announcement-return regressions
outcome: Announcement returns
informs_decision: Q(b): investors value a dollar of revenue surprise more than a dollar of expense surprise, more so for growth firms and with relative persistence of sales vs expenses

citation: Stubben (2010), Discretionary Revenues as a Measure of Earnings Management, The Accounting Review 85(2) 695ff; abstract read
text_source: Annual financial statements; SEC enforcement sample
feature: Discretionary revenue (receivables change not explained by revenue)
method: Simulation and enforcement-sample detection tests
outcome: Detection of manipulation
incremental_to: Accrual models (revenue models less biased and more powerful)
informs_decision: Q(b): receivables growth out of line with revenue is the better manipulation flag; the paper does not test forecasting of future revenue (that use is our hypothesis)

citation: Gow, Larcker and Zakolyukina (2021), Non-Answers During Conference Calls, Journal of Accounting Research 59(4), 1349-1384; working paper of 3 January 2019 read (NYU Stern copy); published abstract checked on EconPapers
text_source: StreetEvents transcripts 2002-2015, US listed non-financial firms with at least five Q&A responses; 18,112 firm-years (2,524 firms) and 2,017,404 question-answer pairs
feature: Explicit non-answers in managers' Q&A responses (Refuse, Unable, After-call); product-related and future-performance-related questions
method: Hand-written regular expressions tuned on 1,296 crowd-coded responses (two CrowdFlower workers per response, RA adjudication), tested on 500 held out: true-positive rate 78.87%, precision 58.95%, accuracy 89.20%; firm-year and within-call regressions
outcome: Non-answer rate (mean 11%) and per-response indicator; future profitability (ROA averaged over t+1 to t+3) enters as a regressor
horizon: Within call; future profitability over three fiscal years
incremental_to: Current ROA, 12-month return, volatility, competition and capital-raising controls; call fixed effects in question-level tests
pit_handling: Not addressed; regexes tuned on random responses, not outcomes; future ROA used by design in a determinant test
informs_decision: Checklist: one SD more future ROA goes with 0.215-0.393 pp fewer non-answers (small); product questions draw refusals for competitive reasons (6.5 pp), so read refusals in context; regexes are a cheap baseline for an LLM labeller; needs the Q&A

citation: Matsumoto, Pronk and Roelofsen (2011), What Makes Conference Calls Useful? The Information Content of Managers' Presentations and Analysts' Discussion Sessions, The Accounting Review 86(4), 1383-1414; read as chapter 2 of Roelofsen's 2010 Erasmus thesis (EPS-2010-190-F&A); published abstract checked
text_source: Over 10,000 earnings calls in trading hours, January 2003 to December 2005 (Voxant via Factiva), NYSE and NASDAQ firms; n = 10,062
feature: Abnormal presentation length; share of financial and forward-looking words in the presentation; discussion (Q&A) length
method: Two-stage firm fixed-effects regressions: residual presentation length (stage 1 R2 0.76) on discussion length; call length on changes in analysts' q+1 forecasts
outcome: Discussion length; absolute revision, accuracy change and dispersion change of analysts' q+1 EPS forecasts against actual q+1 EPS
horizon: Next quarter (q+1), forecasts within 90 days of the call
incremental_to: The press release (published abstract); thesis controls for earnings surprise, performance, special items and firm fixed effects
pit_handling: Not addressed; full-sample residuals with firm fixed effects; no LLM
informs_decision: Text source: what calls add over the release comes mainly through the Q&A; an IQR change in length moves q+1 revisions 6.9% and accuracy 7.6% of their IQRs, driven by discussion length, not presentation length; a prepared-remarks-only arm captures the weaker half

citation: Druz, Petzev, Wagner and Zeckhauser (2020), When Managers Change Their Tone, Analysts and Investors Change Their Tune, Financial Analysts Journal 76(2), 47-69; read as Druz, Wagner and Zeckhauser, Reading Managerial Tone, HKS Working Paper RWP16-004 (January 2016)
text_source: S&P 500 earnings call transcripts 2004-2012 split into presentation, analysts' questions and answers; EDGAR press releases; 13,743 firm-quarters
feature: Residual (unexpected) negativity of presentation and answers after the press release's negativity, performance, pre-call consensus and CEO fixed effects; tone disappointment vs delight; uncertain and modal words, sentence length, atypical tense
method: Loughran-McDonald word counts with negation rule; panel regressions with industry and CEO fixed effects, clustered by CEO
outcome: EPS in quarter t+1; post-call forecast dispersion, revision frequency, spreads; analyst revisions and errors; CAR[0,1] and drift [2,50]
horizon: Next quarter; unreported results to the same quarter next year
incremental_to: Press release negativity, analysts' question negativity, pre-call and post-call (day 3) consensus for t+1
pit_handling: Not addressed; in-sample residuals with CEO fixed effects; no LLM
informs_decision: Checklist rank 1: one SD of presentation residual negativity lowers t+1 EPS by $0.044 (t = -8.33; answers $0.026, t = -5.28; EPS mean 0.73, SD 0.63), still -0.042 after the post-call consensus; in the presentation gloom predicts about twice as much as cheer; works on prepared remarks; analysts' question negativity also predicts (-0.074, t = -6.44)

citation: Lee (2016), Can Investors Detect Managers' Lack of Spontaneity? Adherence to Pre-determined Scripts during Earnings Conference Calls, The Accounting Review 91(1); AAA accepted manuscript read
text_source: Factiva FD Wire earnings calls 2002-2011; 40,820 calls of 2,863 nonfinancial firms; spokesman manager at least 200 words in each part
feature: Q&A scripting: similarity of the spokesman's function-word use in the Q&A and in the prepared remarks, length-adjusted, in deciles; abnormal version net of the manager's prior four quarters
method: LIWC function-word cosine similarity; validation by randomisation (style identifies the manager 79.8% to 87.0% of the time against nine others) and by reading deciles (fewer 'and/so/but' starts, fewer pauses); OLS with manager and year-quarter fixed effects
outcome: Unexpected EPS vs median analyst forecast for t+1, t+2 and both; CAR[0,1], CAR[2,92]; t+1 forecast revisions; spreads; guidance
incremental_to: Current earnings surprise, analysts' forecasts (outcome is relative to them), guidance and guidance surprise, Loughran-McDonald tone, refusals to answer, word counts, tenure
pit_handling: Not addressed; full-sample deciles; the abnormal measure uses only the prior four quarters and gives the same result; no LLM
informs_decision: Checklist: top vs bottom scripting decile has unexpected earnings lower by 0.082 (t+1) and 0.099 (t+2), 29.8% and 28.3% of median magnitudes; analysts revise down; needs both prepared remarks and Q&A; function-word style is a speaker fingerprint (re-identification risk)

citation: Bochkay, Hales and Chava (2020), Hyperbole or Reality? Investor Response to Extreme Language in Earnings Conference Calls, The Accounting Review 95(2), 31-60; typeset article read (AAA newsroom copy)
text_source: Seeking Alpha transcripts 2006-2015: 60,940 calls, 35,155 firm-quarters after filters (36,171 in the performance table); broad US sample
feature: Signed linguistic extremity: share of extreme (|rating| 4-5) vs moderate (1-3) positive and negative words and phrases
method: Dictionary of 23,355 call words and phrases rated -5 to +5 by five MTurk Masters each (ICC 88%, 90.4% after pruning to 13,513; 94.4% correlation with graduate-student ratings); OLS with year-quarter fixed effects, two-way clustering
outcome: Change in sales and in earnings from quarter q to q+4, scaled by assets; BHAR and abnormal volume [0,2]; analyst revisions
incremental_to: Earnings surprise, current ROA and past ROA and sales changes, accruals, firm characteristics, forward-looking/risk/uncertainty/number counts; not the press release or analysts' sales forecasts
pit_handling: Not addressed; dictionary built from all calls but rated without outcomes; in-sample regressions; no LLM
informs_decision: Checklist rank 2 and the only sales outcome: one SD of signed extremity raises the four-quarter sales change by 0.0038 of assets (t = 6.31; median 0.0075, SD 0.0591); extreme negative words strongest; moderate positive words carry nothing; reported to hold in prepared remarks and Q&A separately (appendix not read)

citation: Liang and Carrasco Kind (2025), How do managers' non-responses during earnings calls affect analyst forecasts: a measurement by large language models, arXiv 2505.18419 v1 (PDF read)
text_source: S&P 500 transcripts from Capital IQ, 2019Q1-2024Q3: 10,976 calls, 107,564 analyst-management exchanges; 4,284 calls of 268 firms in regressions
feature: Managers' non-responses per exchange and per call, typed as refusal, lack of info, legal, recall (get back to you), irrelevant; Gricean quantity, relevance and clarity scores
method: GPT-4 (version unstated) and Llama 3.3, temperature 0, few-shot three-task prompt with quoted evidence; prompt tuned to over 70% overlap with 200 hand-coded exchanges; 100 regenerations: 76.22% and 69.11% agreement; GPT-4 flags 23.3% more than Llama
outcome: Analyst forecast error, dispersion and uncertainty after the call; drift, volatility, volume, spreads over 60 days
incremental_to: Firm and quarter fixed effects and firm controls; not the press release
pit_handling: Not addressed; sample inside the models' training period
informs_decision: Checklist (needs Q&A): one SD more non-responses raises forecast error by 11.24% of its mean; only direct refusals matter; refusals add uncertainty rather than a direction; LLM labels on S&P 500 calls are feasible but unstable without a rubric, human check set and repeat runs

citation: Hollander, Pronk and Roelofsen (2010), Does Silence Speak? An Empirical Analysis of Disclosure Choices During Conference Calls, Journal of Accounting Research 48(3), 531-563; abstract read on IDEAS
text_source: Conference call transcripts (sample not stated in the abstract)
feature: Managers not answering participants' questions
method: Not stated in the abstract
outcome: Determinants of non-answers; investor reaction
informs_decision: Non-answers predicted by size, stock-price-based CEO pay, age, performance, litigation risk and analyst activity; investors read silence as bad news; returns only, no fundamentals test in the abstract

citation: Larcker and Zakolyukina (2012), Detecting Deceptive Discussions in Conference Calls, Journal of Accounting Research 50(2), 495-540; abstract read on EconPapers
text_source: Quarterly earnings call transcripts, CEO and CFO narratives
feature: Psycholinguistic word categories linked to deception (general knowledge references, positive and extreme positive emotion, anxiety, shareholder value)
method: Linguistic classification models trained on calls labelled truthful or deceptive from later restatements and severity criteria
outcome: Restatement-based deception label; portfolio alpha
incremental_to: Models on financial and accounting variables (at least equivalent)
pit_handling: Label uses later restatements by construction; out-of-sample tests reported
informs_decision: Low rank for growth: out-of-sample accuracy 6-16% above random; top deception scores (CFO) earn -4% to -11% annual alpha; outcome is misreporting, not sales

citation: Barth, Mansouri and Woebbeking (2023), 'Let Me Get Back to You': A Machine Learning Approach to Measuring NonAnswers, Management Science 69(10), 6333-6348; abstract read on EconPapers, IWH press release 14/2023 read
text_source: S&P 500 earnings call Q&A, 2002-2019, about 1.2 million manager responses (press release)
feature: Non-answers flagged by a glossary of 1,364 trigrams (for example 'I don't know', 'an interesting question', 'back to you')
method: Supervised machine learning (multinomial inverse regression per keywords) on a large labelled set of questions and answers
outcome: Cumulative abnormal returns and implied volatility after the call
informs_decision: Returns and implied volatility only: non-answers go with lower CARs and higher implied volatility; more frequent after harsh and forward-looking questions (press release); no fundamentals test seen

citation: de Kok (2025), ChatGPT for Textual Analysis? How to Use Generative LLMs in Accounting Research, Management Science 71(9), 7888-7906; abstract read on IDEAS and companion repository README read; full text not opened (INFORMS and SSRN returned 403)
text_source: Earnings conference call Q&A (case study)
feature: Non-answers and their dimensions: justification (cannot give, do not know), type (complete refusal, qualitative, range or percentage), question type (breakdown, forward-looking, related party, R&D or regulation), sentiment spin (optimistic vs neutral or pessimistic)
method: GPT-based classification (zero-shot and fine-tuned examples with GPT-4 and Llama 2 70B in the repository); framework for model choice, prompting and construct validity
outcome: Classification accuracy against human labels
incremental_to: Gow et al. (2021) regex measure: 96% accuracy, 70% fewer non-answer errors
informs_decision: LLM measurement: the validated LLM non-answer label, with a richer typology a checklist can borrow; links to fundamentals not in the abstract; stream 02 has a row on the same paper

citation: Davis, Ge, Matsumoto and Zhang (2015), The effect of manager-specific optimism on the tone of earnings conference calls, Review of Accounting Studies 20(2), 639-673; abstract read on IDEAS
text_source: Earnings call transcripts (sample not in the abstract)
feature: Manager-specific component of call tone
method: Tone regressed on current and future performance and strategic incentives; manager effects
outcome: Tone; call-window returns
incremental_to: Current performance, future performance, strategic incentives
informs_decision: Fragility: tone levels carry a manager's personal optimism (linked to early-career experience and charity work), so compare a manager with his own past calls; some evidence investors adjust for it

citation: Mayew and Venkatachalam (2012), The power of voice: Managerial affective states and future firm performance, Journal of Finance 67(1), 1-43; abstract read on Duke Scholars
text_source: Earnings call audio files
feature: Positive and negative vocal affect of managers under analysts' questioning
method: Vocal emotion analysis software
outcome: Future firm performance; analyst forecasts and recommendations
incremental_to: Quantitative earnings information and linguistic content of the call
informs_decision: Out of reach for a text reader: vocal affect predicts the firm's financial future incrementally to words; analysts ignore it in near-term forecasts; tells us what a transcript loses

citation: Cohen, Lou and Malloy (2020), Casting Conference Calls, Management Science 66(11), 5015-5039; abstract read on EconPapers
text_source: Earnings call transcripts in the US, UK, Canada, France and Japan
feature: Whether firms disproportionately call on bullish analysts in the Q&A
method: Analyst participation matched to analysts' views; long-short portfolios
outcome: Future earnings surprises, restatements, returns
informs_decision: Not usable under blinding: casting firms have more negative future earnings surprises and restatements and earn up to 149 bp per month less; needs analyst identities and recommendations, which are identifiers

citation: Price, Doran, Peterson and Bliss (2012), Earnings conference calls and stock returns: The incremental informativeness of textual tone, Journal of Banking & Finance 36(4), 992-1011; abstract read on EconPapers
text_source: Quarterly earnings call transcripts
feature: Call tone; Q&A tone
method: Computer-aided content analysis; context-specific dictionary vs Harvard IV-4
outcome: Abnormal returns, trading volume, post-earnings drift
informs_decision: Returns only: tone dominates earnings surprises over 60 days; the Q&A adds explanatory power for drift, mainly in non-dividend payers; finance-specific dictionaries beat general ones

citation: Bushee, Gow and Taylor (2018), Linguistic Complexity in Firm Disclosures: Obfuscation or Information?, Journal of Accounting Research 56(1), 85-121; abstract read on EconPapers
text_source: Quarterly earnings conference calls
feature: Linguistic complexity split into an information component and an obfuscation component
method: New estimation method for the two latent components
outcome: Information asymmetry
informs_decision: Fragility: raw complexity mixes informative technical content and obfuscation with opposite effects; a reader should not treat long or complex answers as evasion by default

citation: Brockman, Li and Price (2015), Differences in Conference Call Tones: Managers vs. Analysts, Financial Analysts Journal 71(4), 24-42; abstract read on IDEAS
text_source: Quarterly earnings calls, 16 quarters 2004-2007, parsed by speaker
feature: Tone of managers vs tone of analysts
method: Speaker-level text-analysis software
outcome: Investor (institutional and individual) reactions
informs_decision: Analysts' tone moves investors more than managers' tone, and managers sound much more optimistic; supports reading the questions, not only the answers (needs the Q&A)

citation: Chen, Rui and Whinston (2017), Between the Lines: Decipher the Firms' Fundamentals with Artificial Intelligience [sic], manuscript JEB_2017_110 submitted to the 2017 Philadelphia Fed FinTech conference; full text read; unpublished
text_source: 6,554 S&P 500 transcripts, 2011 to June 2015; LDA fitted on over 0.25 million Q&A rounds 2010 to June 2015
feature: Evasiveness = topic-distribution cosine similarity between an analyst's questions and the answers in a round (higher = more on topic); incoherence (word2vec); emotional inconsistency between prepared remarks and answers (LIWC)
method: LDA (K = 30) and word embeddings; validation: 67 undergraduates rated documents, overlap with the measure 82% (most evasive quartile) and 69% (least) vs 25% by chance; pooled OLS with firm fixed effects
outcome: Next-quarter SUE (seasonal random walk) and standardised analyst forecast error (SAFE)
incremental_to: Lagged SUE, forecast dispersion and revisions, size, book-to-market, turnover, momentum and pre-announcement returns
pit_handling: Not addressed; topic model fitted on the full sample period
informs_decision: Weak support for evasion as a fundamentals signal on our universe: a 4-SD move in Q-A similarity shifts next-quarter SUE by about 0.145 SD; R2 0.109 to 0.148 with three text measures; table inconsistencies and an ambiguous SUE timing, so low weight

citation: Kim, Muhn and Nikolaev, From Transcripts to Insights: Uncovering Corporate Risks Using Generative AI, arXiv 2310.17721 v2 (19 March 2025); abstract read
text_source: Earnings call transcripts (stream 02 row: Capital IQ, 2018 to March 2023)
feature: Political, climate and AI risk exposure from GPT-3.5 risk summaries and assessments
method: GPT-3.5 prompts per risk type
outcome: Firm-level (abnormal) volatility, investment, innovation; pricing in equity markets
pit_handling: Abstract: measures work within and outside GPT's training window; method not described in the abstract
informs_decision: LLM measurement: call-derived LLM scores predict real choices (investment) as well as volatility, with an outside-window check; outcome is not sales; stream 02 has a fuller row

outcome: EPS beat or miss

citation: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock and Mellers (2025), Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities, arXiv 2506.01578 v1 (PDF read in full)
text_source: 100 binary ForecastBench questions (2024-12-08 set) resolving December 2024; FRED, Yahoo Finance, Metaculus, Polymarket and others; no documents
feature: Probability under 37 single-element prompts (Study 1) and 17 compound, vendor-generated and literature prompts (Study 2) against one minimal control
method: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B at temperature 0; o1 and o1-mini in Study 2; pre-registered mixed model on per-item Brier differences with Benjamini-Hochberg correction; t-tests as secondary
outcome: Brier score
pit_handling: Vendor-stated cutoffs (Oct 2023 to Jul 2024) all before resolution; no between-model comparison
informs_decision: Expected playbook gain: best single prompts -0.011 to -0.019 Brier, not robust; compound prompts no better (best -0.009, n.s.); Bayesian updating +0.030, propose-evaluate-select +0.033, expert odds-ratio protocol +0.023 (all worse); persona n.s.; base-rate prompts the only consistent small gain; reasoning models same pattern

citation: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han and Steinhardt (2024), Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models, arXiv 2402.18563 v1 (HTML read)
text_source: 5,516 binary questions from Metaculus, GJOpen, INFER, Polymarket, Manifold (914 test, opened after cutoff); date-filtered news retrieval
feature: Probability from a retrieval-augmented system with a scratchpad prompt chosen from 15, a fine-tuned reasoner and a trimmed-mean ensemble
method: GPT-4-1106-Preview base and fine-tuned GPT-4-0613; prompt and hyperparameters chosen on validation; ablations removing fine-tuning and retrieval; five ensembling rules compared
outcome: Brier score; accuracy; RMS calibration error
horizon: Platform question horizons, five retrieval dates each
incremental_to: Human crowd (0.149); zero-shot and scratchpad baselines of 14 models
pit_handling: Test questions open after stated cutoff; train and validation resolved before; retrieval date-filtered; manual post-training leakage probe
informs_decision: Prompt structure alone is worth about 0.002 Brier (0.206 v 0.208 zero-shot); scratchpad no better than zero-shot without retrieval (GPT-4 0.209 v 0.208); averaging 6 samples -0.003, LLM aggregator +0.0015; system hedges and rarely gives low probabilities; select prompts on validation, test later in time

citation: Pratt, Blumberg, Kreitlon Carolino and Morris (2024), Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?, arXiv 2406.04446 v1 (HTML read)
text_source: GleanGen internal prediction market (Google); 351 validation and 341 test events; 78 open on 1 August 2022
feature: Probability under human forecasting strategies (breakdown, base rates, both sides, persona crowd, news) chained as LLM modules
method: PaLM 2 (pre-training ended July 2022); Brier, class-weighted Brier; with and without rationale; reversed-event coherence probe
outcome: Brier score; weighted Brier
horizon: From 1 August 2022 to resolution (many end of 2022)
incremental_to: Basic one-prompt baseline; human market midpoint
pit_handling: Model with known pre-training end; forecast date set just after it
informs_decision: No strategy beat the basic prompt (0.1221; breakdown 0.1895, base rates 0.1562); asking for a rationale raised probabilities across events; P(event) + P(not event) well below 1; check base rate and level shifts, not Brier alone

citation: Turpin, Michael, Perez and Bowman (2023), Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting, NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.04388 v2 (HTML read)
text_source: BIG-Bench Hard (13 tasks, 3,299 examples); BBQ (2,592 questions with weak evidence)
feature: Answer and chain-of-thought explanation under injected biasing features (suggested answer; answer always A; stereotypes)
method: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0; chain of thought v direct; zero-shot v few-shot; paired accuracy differences; hand annotation of explanations
outcome: Accuracy drop biased v unbiased; share of unfaithful pairs explained by stereotype
incremental_to: Same inputs without the biasing feature; no chain of thought
pit_handling: Not addressed (the biasing feature plays the role of a remembered outcome)
informs_decision: Hidden influences move answers by up to 36.3 points while explanations never mention them (1 of 426); 73% of unfaithful explanations argue for the biased answer; zero-shot reasoning can amplify the bias (39.5 to 23.3%); matches EXP-0029: stated reasons cannot audit the S2 call

citation: Lanham, Chen, Radhakrishnan and 27 others (2023), Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning, arXiv 2307.13702 v1 (HTML read)
text_source: Eight multiple-choice tasks (AQuA, LogiQA, MMLU, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, OpenBookQA, ARC Challenge and Easy)
feature: Dependence of the answer on the reasoning: early answering, added mistakes, filler tokens, paraphrase; by model size
method: 175B RLHF dialogue model, 100 sampled reasonings per question; Ganguli et al. size series for scaling
outcome: Share of answers unchanged after intervention (AOC); accuracy with v without reasoning
informs_decision: Reasoning is often post-hoc (early-answering AOC 0.02 to 0.44 by task); dependence unrelated to accuracy gain; larger models less faithful on 7 of 8 tasks; gives the truncation and edit tests for checking whether S2 probabilities depend on playbook output

citation: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez and seven others (2025), To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2409.12183 v3 (HTML read)
text_source: Meta-analysis of 110 papers (1,218 comparisons); own runs on 20 datasets with 14 models
feature: Accuracy of chain of thought v direct answer by task type; planning v execution v tool solver
method: Zero- and few-shot prompting, greedy decoding; paired bootstrap with Bonferroni; MMLU split by presence of '='; Python and Z3 solvers
outcome: Accuracy
pit_handling: GSM8K-Hard used against contamination; otherwise not addressed
informs_decision: Chain of thought helps math and symbolic tasks (+14.2, +12.3, +6.9 points) and little elsewhere (56.8 v 56.1); tools beat chain of thought at execution; so compute S2 arithmetic in code and expect little from free-text reasoning on judgement items; compare at matched compute

citation: Kim, Muhn and Nikolaev (2024), Financial Statement Analysis with Large Language Models, arXiv 2407.17866 v2 (HTML read for the prompt ablation only); withdrawn by the authors in v3
text_source: Standardised, anonymised Compustat statements; analyst sample and full sample 1968-2021
feature: Direction of next-year earnings from GPT-4 Turbo with a simple prompt v an analyst-style chain-of-thought prompt (trends, ratios with formulae, interpretation, prediction)
method: Same model and inputs, two prompts
outcome: Directional accuracy; F1
pit_handling: Firm and year guessing near zero; withdrawn for data and analysis inconsistencies; Levy (2026, stream 08) attributes this kind of accuracy to recall
informs_decision: Analyst-step CoT 60.35% v simple prompt 52.33% (+8 points) is the most-cited finance case for an analyst playbook and carries no weight: withdrawn, not reproduced by Li et al. (2024), and consistent with CoT amplifying recall (EXP-0029)

citation: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park and Tetlock (2024), Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy, arXiv 2402.19379 v6 (abstract read; Science Advances 10(45) per the reference list of Schoenegger et al. 2025)

feature: Aggregate of twelve LLMs' probabilities; GPT-4 and Claude 2 updating on the human median
method: Pre-registered comparison with the human crowd; equivalence tests
outcome: Brier score
pit_handling: Questions resolved after the forecasts (live tournament)
informs_decision: Aggregating many models matched the human crowd; models showed an acquiescence bias (mean forecast above 50% with balanced outcomes); seeing the human median improved accuracy 17% to 28%; supports averaging over samples or models

citation: Tian, Mitchell, Zhou, Sharma, Rafailov, Yao, Finn and Manning (2023), Just Ask for Calibration, EMNLP 2023, arXiv 2305.14975 v2 (abstract read)

method: ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude; several elicitation prompts
outcome: Expected calibration error
informs_decision: Verbalised probabilities are often better calibrated than token probabilities (ECE down about 50% relative); supports asking the PM for a stated number

citation: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He and Hooi (2024), Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2306.13063 v2 (abstract read)

method: Five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat; calibration and failure prediction
outcome: ECE; AUROC
informs_decision: Verbalised confidence is overconfident; consistency across multiple sampled answers and better aggregation reduce overconfidence; no method dominates; professional-knowledge tasks remain hard

citation: Fu, Conde, Martínez, Grandury and Reviriego (2026), Multiple Choice Questions: Reasoning Makes Large Language Models (LLMs) More Self-Confident, Especially When They are Wrong, IEEE Intelligent Systems 2026, arXiv 2501.09775 v3 (abstract of v3 and HTML of v2 read)
text_source: MMLU, 57 subjects
feature: Probability of the chosen option with direct answer v reasoning first
method: Seven LLMs; token probabilities; ECE and Brier
outcome: Confidence; ECE; Brier
informs_decision: Reasoning first raises confidence for every model, more when the answer is wrong, and degrades calibration; with Pratt (2024), expect a reasons-first playbook to push S2 probabilities outward

citation: Kanishka and Mandora (2026), Structure Tax: How Structured Output affects LLMs Performance, AACL-IJCNLP 2026 (long), pages 4620-4644 (PDF read, sections 1 to 5)
text_source: GSM8K, MMLU, LogicBench, Spider
feature: Accuracy and calibration under JSON or XML outputs with the reasoning field before or after the answer field, against free form
method: GPT-4o, Gemini Flash 2.0, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B; temperature 0; five runs; prompt-perturbation robustness
outcome: Accuracy; ECE of verbal 1-10 confidence
informs_decision: Reasoning-first fields match or beat free form; answer-first collapses multi-step arithmetic (GSM8K: small models 10.98% v 83% to 87%; the reasoning-first lead was at least 37 points in every perturbation cell, GPT-4o included); XML beat JSON by up to 12.2 points; reasoning-first XML lowered ECE against free text for most models; a structured form is safe if reasoning precedes each answer, and answer-first is risky wherever the model must compute

citation: Chiang and Lee (2023), A Closer Look into Automatic Evaluation Using Large Language Models, Findings of EMNLP 2023, arXiv 2310.05657 v1 (PDF read, section 3)
text_source: SummEval and Topical-Chat meta-evaluation sets
feature: Correlation of ChatGPT ratings with human ratings under score only, rate-explain (rating then explanation) and analyze-rate (analysis then rating)
method: ChatGPT; G-Eval auto chain of thought compared; temperatures 0.3 and 0.7; prompt variants
outcome: Pearson and Kendall correlation with human ratings
informs_decision: Asking for an explanation after the rating helped as much as analysis before it; the rating cannot depend on the later text, so knowing an explanation is due changed the rating; supports a probability-first, reasons-after arm for judgement items

citation: Chen, Benton, Radhakrishnan and twelve others (2025), Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think, arXiv 2505.05410 v1 (abstract and HTML sections 1 to 3 read)
text_source: Prompts with six kinds of embedded hints
feature: Whether reasoning models verbalise hints they use
method: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1 against Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) and DeepSeek V3; MMLU and GPQA prompt pairs with and without a hint; temperature 0; outcome-based RL experiments
outcome: Hint reveal rate
informs_decision: Reasoning models verbalise hints they use in 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1) of cases; unfaithful traces are longer than faithful ones; RL raises faithfulness then plateaus; a frontier model's reasoning cannot rule out use of remembered outcomes, and length is no sign of honesty

citation: Arcuschin, Janiak, Krzyzanowski, Rajamanoharan, Nanda and Conmy (2026), Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful, ICML 2026, arXiv 2503.08679 v6 (abstract read)

method: Production and thinking models
outcome: Rate of contradictory pairs justified by coherent reasoning
informs_decision: Rationalisation of an implicit bias occurs without any injected bias, up to 13% in production models and 0.04% to 0.37% in thinking models; reversed-question pairs are a cheap detector (same idea as the S2 coherence probe)

citation: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo and Griffiths (2025), Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse, arXiv 2410.21333 v4 (abstract read)

citation: Nitarach, Sirichotedumrong, Pitchayarthorn, Taveekitworachai, Manakul and Pipatanakul (2025), FinCoT: Grounding Chain-of-Thought in Expert Financial Reasoning, FinNLP 2025 at EMNLP, arXiv 2506.16123 v5 (abstract read)

citation: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov and Suhr (2024), Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.11324 v2 (abstract read)

citation: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee and Jurgens (2024), When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performances of Large Language Models, Findings of EMNLP 2024, arXiv 2311.10054 v3 (abstract read)

citation: Dhawka, Wilson and Head (2026), Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots, arXiv 2611.12834 v1 (abstract read)

citation: Shetty, Upadhayaya, Shah, Nayak, Fee & Jagabathula (2025), FinLLM@IJCAI 2025, arXiv 2507.02954v2. Read: v2 HTML

citation: Zhang, Cao & Liao (2025), Findings of ACL 2025, pp. 8715-8758 (XFinBench). Read: ACL Anthology page and arXiv 2508.15861v1 HTML (first two-thirds)

citation: Ben Yoash, Brief, Ovadia, Shenderovitz, Mishaeli, Lemberg & Sheetrit (2025), GEM2 workshop at ACL 2025; arXiv 2504.04596v1 (SECQUE). Read: abstract page and v1 HTML

citation: Koncel-Kedziorski, Krumdick, Lai, Reddy, Lovering & Tanner (2024), arXiv 2311.06602v2 (BizBench). Read: abstract page

citation: Reddy, Koncel-Kedziorski, Lai, Krumdick, Lovering & Tanner (2024), arXiv 2401.06915v3 (DocFinQA). Read: abstract page

outcome: Closed-book 39.49 (base) -> 56.22 (EntiGraph 455M tokens) vs GPT-4 51.30; raw CPT below base; rephrase scales poorly; log-linear in synthetic tokens, no plateau reached; with RAG 62.60 vs 60.35
pit_handling: Not relevant (fiction/journalism); method memorises the corpus by design
informs_decision: Document-grounded synthesis teaches a model what a corpus says where raw text does not, with returns rising in volume; diversity from prompt structure (entity pairs). Knowledge, not reasoning; generator faithfulness credited to gpt-4-turbo

citation: Cheng, Gu, Huang, Bi, Huang & Wei (2024), EMNLP 2024; arXiv 2406.14491v2 (Instruction Pre-Training). Read: abstract and v2 HTML (about 92%)

outcome: Finance avg: Llama3-8B 70.1, raw CPT 72.0, Instruct PT 74.7, Llama3-70B 71.9; rule-mined 73.1; 500M 45.1->46.6, 1.3B 48.6->49.7 (9-benchmark avg); finance pairs correct 69.8% (GPT-4 judge), 73.5% (human)
incremental_to: Raw-text continued pre-training; rule-based task mining (AdaptLLM); Llama3-70B
pit_handling: Not addressed; finance corpus undated in text read and not public
informs_decision: A 7B generator writing many short varied tasks per domain document beats raw-text training in finance, and model-written tasks beat rule-mined ones; gain survives ~30% wrong pairs. Closest published design to 'teacher writes many Q&A per 8-K release'

citation: Liu, Bubeck, Eldan, Kulkarni, Li, Nguyen, Ward & Zhang (2023), arXiv 2312.09241v1 (TinyGSM), preprint. Read: abstract and v1 HTML
text_source: Comparable domain (math): 12.3M GPT-3.5-turbo problems with Python solutions (~1.8B tokens, ~$3,600) seeded from 7,473 GSM8K train questions; 13-gram contamination check

outcome: Generator alone: 125M 63.1, 350M 65.9, 1.3B 68.2; 1.3B+1.3B verifier 81.5 vs GPT-3.5 teacher 77.4; 125M gen + 1.3B verifier 76.1 > 1.3B gen + 125M verifier 71.7; 1/3 -> 2/3 of data '10% increase' (points or relative not stated), last third marginal; SVAMP 75.6
incremental_to: Random-init students; larger open models; teacher
pit_handling: n-gram decontamination (22 of 11.0M at 13-gram); paraphrase contamination unsolved

citation: Guha, Marten, Keh, Raoof, Smyrnis, Bansal and 44 others (2025), arXiv 2506.04178v2 (OpenThoughts), preprint. Read: abstract and v2 HTML (about 86%)

outcome: Teacher QwQ-32B > DeepSeek-R1 (code 44.2 vs 42.3; math 44.2 vs 41.6; science 53.2 vs 46.7); 16 answers/question >= more questions; top-2 code sources 41.3 vs top-16 36.4; answer verification no gain (41.9 all vs 40.0 GPT-verified); scaling continues to 1.2M; truncating traces >2,048 tokens -33.3% at 7B

citation: Hsieh, Li, Yeh, Nakhost, Fujii, Ratner, Krishna, Lee & Pfister (2023), Findings of ACL 2023; arXiv 2305.02301v2 (Distilling step-by-step). Read: abstract page and Anthology PDF text (parts)

citation: Ho, Schmid & Yun (2023), ACL 2023; arXiv 2212.10071v2 (Large Language Models Are Reasoning Teachers). Read: abstract page and Anthology PDF text (Table 1, Section on diverse reasoning)

informs_decision: Teaching the student to choose among several answer strategies, rather than one template, is an explicit design against template lock-in; students 7B+

citation: Ye, Huang, Xiao, Chern, Xia & Liu (2025), COLM 2025; arXiv 2502.03387v3 (LIMO). Read: abstract and v3 HTML

citation: Muennighoff, Yang, Shi, Li, Fei-Fei, Hajishirzi, Zettlemoyer, Liang, Candes & Hashimoto (2025), arXiv 2501.19393v3 (s1), preprint. Read: abstract and v3 HTML (about 70%)

citation: Busbridge, Shidani, Weers, Ramapuram, Littwin & Webb (2025), ICML 2025; arXiv 2502.08606v2 (Distillation Scaling Laws). Read: abstract and v2 HTML (first 30%)

outcome: Capacity gap: past a point a stronger teacher gives a worse student (U-shape in teacher size, driven by teacher cross-entropy); distillation beats supervised learning only below a compute level that grows with student size, or when a teacher already exists
informs_decision: Teacher too far above student hurts; with existing teachers (S1's case) distillation is the efficient choice at small compute

citation: Cheng, Huang & Wei (2024), ICLR 2024; arXiv 2309.09530v4 (AdaptLLM, reading comprehension). Read: abstract and v4 HTML

citation: Zhang, Wang & Charton (2024), arXiv 2402.10891v1 (Instruction Diversity Drives Generalization To Unseen Tasks), preprint. Read: abstract and v1 HTML
text_source: Synthetic string-rewriting tasks (Markov-algorithm rules); encrypted rewriting with Llama-2-7b
feature: Number of distinct instructions vs examples per instruction, at fixed budget (~10^6 examples); semantic classes of rules
method: Small GPT-2 from scratch; Llama-2-7b LoRA
outcome: No generalisation to unseen instructions below ~300 instructions at ~10^6 examples; transition ~400-500; always generalises at >=1,000 even with few examples each; models trained on few instructions default to the no-op answer; one semantic class of rules does not generalise, a mix does; long-tailed instruction mixes hurt at 1,000 instructions, little at 10^4-10^5
incremental_to: Fewer instructions with more examples each
informs_decision: Diversity of task types, not volume per type, buys transfer to unseen tasks; low diversity makes the model fall back on a default output (cf. S1's boxed number on 300/300 label items)

citation: Fu, Peng, Ou, Sabharwal & Khot (2023), ICML 2023, PMLR 202:10421-10430; arXiv 2301.12726v1 (Specializing Smaller Language Models towards Multi-Step Reasoning). Read: PMLR page and arXiv PDF text (Sections 1-4)
text_source: Comparable domain (math): GSM8K 7K questions x 40 code-davinci-002 solutions, correct kept = 130K

outcome: FlanT5 gains ~+10 on math (11B GSM8K 16.1 -> 27.1; 4-set avg 40.8 vs LaMDA-137B 35.9); BBH CoT drops to 0 at the first checkpoint; zero-shot-format data removes in-context ability, in-context data keeps both; FlanT5-3B plateaus ~90K examples, smaller models need more epochs; in-dist vs OOD checkpoint choice trades ~2 points
informs_decision: A small model can beat much larger ones on one skill by giving up generic ability; the format of training data decides which abilities survive. Matches S1's FinQA drop and single-format lock-in

informs_decision: For sub-4B students a larger teacher is not reliably better; same-family teachers help; compatibility with the student predicts usefulness

citation: Zhang, Li, Song, Ye, Gao & Hu (2025), ACL 2025; arXiv 2311.07052v4 (Towards the Law of Capacity Gap in Distilling Language Models). Read: abstract and v4 HTML (about 75%)

outcome: Optimal teacher T* ~ 2.5 x student (fit 2.498 S - 11.498, R2 0.996); MiniMA degrades when the teacher grows from LLaMA2-7B to 13B and 70B
informs_decision: For a 0.8B student the optimum under this law is ~2B; 4B is ~5x. Fit on pre-training-style logit KD, not reasoning SFT

citation: Chen, Sun, Guo, Zhang, Chen, Sun, Su, Pan, Klakow, Li & Shen (2025), Findings of ACL 2025; arXiv 2502.18001v3 (Unveiling the Key Factors for Distilling Chain-of-Thought Reasoning). Read: abstract and v3 HTML (about 88%)

informs_decision: For students near 1B, keep traces simple and pick the teacher empirically; teacher accuracy is a weak guide

citation: Agarwal, Vieillard, Zhou, Stanczyk, Ramos, Geist & Bachem (2024), ICLR 2024; arXiv 2306.13649v3 (GKD: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models). Read: abstract and v3 HTML
